content: The report titled Research Priorities for Zoonoses and Marginalized Infections is part of the WHO Technical Report Series (No. 971) and represents the collective views of an international group of experts. It does not necessarily reflect the decisions or policies of the World Health Organization (WHO). This document provides a comprehensive review and analysis of the research landscape for zoonotic diseases and marginalized infectious diseases that disproportionately affect impoverished populations. It also outlines research priorities aimed at supporting disease control efforts. The work is the result of the Disease Reference Group on Zoonoses and Marginalized Infectious Diseases of Poverty (DRG6), which is an independent think tank of international experts established and funded by the Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Diseases (TDR). The group was tasked with identifying key research priorities through a systematic review of existing research evidence and consultations with stakeholders. The report addresses a wide range of diseases, including zoonotic helminth, protozoan, viral, and bacterial infections that are often neglected and associated with poverty. Disease-specific research issues are detailed in individual sections, and common priorities across diseases are identified. These include the need for new or improved drugs, diagnostic tools, and, where applicable, vaccines. The disease-specific priorities are described as micro priorities, which focus on specific diseases, in contrast to macro-level priorities that guide policymaking. These macro priorities include improving surveillance systems, fostering collaboration between health, livestock, agriculture, natural resources, and wildlife sectors, and accurately assessing the burden of zoonotic diseases. The WHO, established in 1948 as a specialized agency of the United Nations, serves as the directing and coordinating authority for international health matters. One of its constitutional functions is to provide objective and reliable information and advice in the field of human health. This responsibility is fulfilled in part through its extensive program of publications, which aim to support national health strategies and address pressing public health concerns globally. WHO publications include practical manuals, handbooks, training materials, internationally applicable guidelines, reviews, and analyses of health policies, as well as state-of-the-art consensus reports offering technical advice and recommendations for decision-makers. These publications are closely aligned with the organization's priority activities, such as disease prevention and control, the development of equitable health systems based on primary health care, and health promotion for individuals and communities. The WHO Technical Report Series disseminates the findings of various international expert groups that provide the organization with the latest scientific and technical advice on a broad range of medical and public health subjects. Members of these expert groups serve in their personal capacities without remuneration and do not represent governments or other bodies. Their views do not necessarily reflect the decisions or stated policies of WHO. The Disease Reference Group on Zoonoses and Marginalized Infectious Diseases of Poverty (DRG6) was established to address the limited recognition by the global health community of zoonoses and marginalized infectious diseases as major causes of poverty and constraints on development. The group reviewed these diseases and provided an analysis of research priorities. The report emphasizes the diversity of the diseases discussed, which range from viral to parasitic infections. These infections exhibit various transmission patterns, have a global distribution across tropical and subtropical regions, and exist in different ecological environments and health system settings. The complexity of addressing these diseases is compounded by the need to involve multiple sectors, such as livestock services, education, environment, water and sanitation, and wildlife, in decision-making, policy development, and implementation of research findings. The group also highlighted cross-disease and thematic issues through interactions with stakeholders and the WHO Secretariat. A series of matrices was developed to evaluate research priorities from the perspective of cross-cutting themes. This approach aimed to recognize the complexity of priority-setting and to address the challenges of implementing research findings, particularly for diseases that primarily affect marginalized populations with limited access to government services. The group identified two levels of prioritization. First, disease-specific and focused priorities were addressed, driven by appropriate biomedical or social paradigms. These recommendations are extensive and relevant to disease-focused scientific constituencies. Second, broader priorities emerged that are relevant to the different diseases considered in the report and infectious diseases in general. Biomedical priorities were identified for specific diseases, drawing on expert opinions, stakeholder discussions, and existing published material from WHO and other authoritative groups. These priorities include the need for new drugs, diagnostics, and human and animal vaccines. Macro priorities for policymakers were also identified, covering all the diseases included in the analysis. These include expanding surveillance for zoonotic diseases in humans and animals, re-attributing the burden of morbidity and mortality to neglected parasitic/zoonotic diseases, re-evaluating the societal burden of zoonoses, expanding systems research to improve intersectoral collaboration, evaluating the effectiveness of community-led approaches, integrating animal and human disease expertise with social science perspectives, conducting cost-effectiveness studies, scaling up research training to increase human resources in public health and veterinary services, creating opportunities to evaluate and modify control strategies, combining interventions with improved water and sanitation, and expanding research on the use of new communication technologies for surveillance and reporting. The conclusions and deliberations of the DRG are summarized in the report, specifying disease-specific priorities versus broader macro priorities. The report also highlights the importance of fostering a global research effort on infectious diseases of poverty, with endemic countries playing a pivotal role. This effort involves systematic reviews of evidence, assessment of research needs, and periodic consultations with national and regional stakeholders to set research priorities for accelerating the control of these diseases.
